'''Sabine Karin Doris Hossenfelder''' is a German [[science communicator]], writer, and [[YouTuber]] who previously worked as an academic [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]].<ref name=":0">{{cite news |last=Neuman |first=Scott |date=23 September 2023 |title=She got famous on YouTube. Now it helps fund her research in quantum gravity |url=https://laist.com/news/npr-news/she-got-famous-on-youtube-now-it-helps-fund-her-research-in-quantum-gravity |access-date=11 September 2026 |work=[[NPR]] |via=LAist}}</ref><ref name="Wolchover2026">{{cite web |last=Wolchover |first=Natalie |title=Are Strings Still Our Best Hope for a Theory of Everything? |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/are-strings-still-our-best-hope-for-a-theory-of-everything-20260323/ |website=Quanta Magazine |date=23 March 2026 |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> After working as an academic physicist for two decades, Hossenfelder rose to prominence on YouTube in the early 2020s.<ref name=":0" /> By September 2026, her channel had 1.79 million subscribers.<ref name="sb" /> Hossenfelder is known for her controversial criticism of modern physics research.<ref name="Schulz2024" /><ref name=":1" />

== Early life and education ==
Hossenfelder was born in [[Frankfurt]].<ref name="guardian">{{cite news |last=Fox |first=Killian |title=Physicist Sabine Hossenfelder: 'There are quite a few areas where physics blurs into religion' |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2022/nov/26/physicist-sabine-hossenfelder-there-are-quite-a-few-areas-where-physics-blurs-into-religion-multiverse |work=The Guardian |date=26 November 2022 |access-date=11 July 2025}}</ref> She studied mathematics and physics at Goethe University Frankfurt.<ref name="fias2019" /> Hossenfelder later earned a doctorate from the same university in theoretical physics in 2003; her dissertation, supervised by [[Horst Stöcker]], studied microscopic black-hole production in models with large extra dimensions.<ref>{{cite web |title=Schwarze Löcher in Extra-Dimensionen : Eigenschaften und Nachweis |url=https://publikationen.ub.uni-frankfurt.de/frontdoor/index/index/docId/5305 |website=Goethe-University publication server |year=2003 |access-date=11 July 2025}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
After post-doctoral posts at the [[GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research]], [[University of Arizona]], [[University of California, Santa Barbara|UC Santa Barbara]] and [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics|Perimeter Institute]] in Canada,<ref name="fias2019" /><ref name="nordita2009" /> she joined [[NORDITA]] in Stockholm as an assistant professor in 2009.<ref name="nordita2009" /> In 2015, she moved to the [[Frankfurt Institute for Advanced Studies]], where she led the Analog Systems for Gravity Duals group and, in 2019, received the institute's inaugural Award for Innovative Thinking.<ref name="fias2019" /> In 2023, she became affiliated with the [[LMU Munich]] Center for Mathematical Philosophy as a visiting researcher, studying the role of locality and fine-tuning in quantum-mechanical foundations.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="mcmp" /> In September 2025, Hossenfelder said that she was no longer affiliated with the center.<ref name="affiliation2025">{{cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZO5u3V6LJuM |title=I can't believe this really happened. |date=17 September 2025 |last=Hossenfelder |first=Sabine |access-date=11 September 2026 |via=YouTube}}</ref>

Hossenfelder has published research on topics such as [[quantum gravity]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hossenfelder |first=Sabine |date=29 January 2013 |title=Minimal Length Scale Scenarios for Quantum Gravity |journal=Living Reviews in Relativity |language=en |volume=16 |issue=1 |article-number=2 |doi=10.12942/lrr-2013-2 |doi-access=free |issn=2367-3613 |pmc=5255898 |pmid=28179841 |arxiv=1203.6191 |bibcode=2013LRR....16....2H }}</ref> [[black hole]]s,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hossenfelder |first1=S. |last2=Smolin |first2=L. |date=2010-03-05 |title=Conservative solutions to the black hole information problem |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.81.064009 |journal=Physical Review D |language=en |volume=81 |issue=6 |article-number=064009 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.81.064009 |arxiv=0901.3156 |bibcode=2010PhRvD..81f4009H |issn=1550-7998}}</ref> and [[dark matter]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Khelashvili |first1=M |last2=Rudakovskyi |first2=A |last3=Hossenfelder |first3=S |date=2023-06-08 |title=Dark matter profiles of SPARC galaxies: a challenge to fuzzy dark matter |url=https://academic.oup.com/mnras/article/523/3/3393/7186934 |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |language=en |volume=523 |issue=3 |pages=3393–3405 |doi=10.1093/mnras/stad1595 |doi-access=free |issn=0035-8711 |url-access=subscription|arxiv=2207.14165 }}</ref>

== Public engagement ==
Hossenfelder has written the popular-science blog ''Backreaction'' since 2006 and has contributed articles to ''[[Scientific American]]'', ''[[New Scientist]]'' and ''[[Quanta Magazine]]''.<ref name="fias2019" /> Her first trade book, ''Lost in Math: How Beauty Leads Physics Astray'' (Basic Books, 2018), argues that an aesthetic preference for mathematically "beautiful" theories has hindered progress in fundamental physics.<ref>{{cite journal |author-link=Anil Ananthaswamy |last=Ananthaswamy |first=Anil |title=How the belief in beauty has triggered a crisis in physics |date=12 June 2018 |journal=Nature |volume=558 |issue=7709 |pages=186–187 |doi=10.1038/d41586-018-05374-9 |bibcode=2018Natur.558..186A |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-018-05374-9 |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> Her follow-up, ''[[Existential Physics: A Scientist's Guide to Life's Biggest Questions]]'', was published by Viking in 2022,<ref>{{cite web |title=Existential Physics |url=https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/667013/existential-physics-by-sabine-hossenfelder/ |website=Penguin Random House |access-date=11 July 2025}}</ref> exploring what physics can say about questions such as [[free will]], consciousness and the origin of the universe. In a positive review, ''[[Kirkus Reviews]]'' stated that the book suggests that "many spiritual ideas are compatible with modern physics".<ref>{{cite web |date=10 May 2022 |title=Existential Physics |url=https://www.kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/sabine-hossenfelder/existential-physics/ |website=Kirkus Reviews |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref>

During the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] in the early 2020s, Hossenfelder began focusing on YouTube content explaining science in simple terms. By September 2023, her channel had reached one million subscribers, and NPR reported that income from YouTube helped fund her physics research.<ref name=":0" /> By November 2024, creating YouTube videos had become her main activity, while she devoted less time to physics research.<ref name="Schulz2024">{{cite news |last=Schulz |first=Peter |title=“Eu não sou líder de torcida da ciência” |trans-title=I am not a science cheerleader |url=https://jornal.unicamp.br/artigo/2024/11/14/peter-schulz/eu-nao-sou-lider-de-torcida-da-ciencia-diz-sabine-hossenfelder/ |work=Jornal da Unicamp |date=14 November 2024 |language=pt |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> As of September 2026, her channel had reached 1.79 million subscribers and approximately 378 million total views.<ref name="sb" />

Hossenfelder is known for her strong criticism of modern academic physics research.<ref name=":2" />

NPR described Hossenfelder's views on modern physics research as "somewhat contrarian".<ref name=":0" /> She has written op-eds in ''[[The Guardian]]'' and ''[[The New York Times]]'' critiquing [[particle physics]] and the search for hypothesized particles using [[collider]]s.<ref>{{cite news |last=Hossenfelder |first=Sabine |date=26 September 2022 |title=No one in physics dares say so, but the race to invent new particles is pointless |url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2022/sep/26/physics-particles-physicists |access-date=11 September 2026 |work=The Guardian}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Hossenfelder |first=Sabine |date=23 January 2019 |title=The Uncertain Future of Particle Physics |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/01/23/opinion/particle-physics-large-hadron-collider.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref> Responding in a published letter, cosmologist Phil Bull argued that unsuccessful searches also advance science by testing hypotheses and excluding possibilities.<ref>{{cite news |last=Bull |first=Phil |title=Particle physics – a brief history of time-wasting? |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2022/sep/30/particle-physics-a-brief-history-of-time-wasting |work=The Guardian |date=30 September 2022 |access-date=11 September 2026 |type=Letter}}</ref> Hossenfelder has been criticised by science communicators for her anti-establishment and pessimistic presentation of academia, arguing that it could aid science denialists.<ref name="Schulz2024" /> In 2024, Hossenfelder described [[string theory]] as "undead", but weeks later said that a paper using bootstrapping methods strengthened the argument for the theory.<ref name="Wolchover2026" />

Writing for McGill University's Office for Science and Society in April 2025, [[Jonathan Jarry]] praised Hossenfelder's ability to explain complex science but criticised her broader claims about academic research. He argued that her criticism had expanded from particle physics to claims that science itself was failing, and that her portrayal of publicly funded research as a scam was misleading and risked undermining public trust in science. He also wrote that her videos criticising academic research tended to attract more views than her educational videos.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |last=Jarry |first=Jonathan |date=18 April 2025 |title=Sabine Hossenfelder Asks If Science Is Dying. It's Not. |url=https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/critical-thinking-general-science/sabine-hossenfelder-asks-if-science-dying-its-not |access-date=11 September 2026 |website=Office for Science and Society |publisher=McGill University}}</ref> In a September 2025 essay in ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'', Dan Kagan-Kans described Hossenfelder as part of a genre of "conspiracy physics" YouTubers who portray academic physics as a corrupt establishment.<ref name=":2">{{cite news |last=Kagan-Kans |first=Dan |date=11 September 2025 |title=The Rise of 'Conspiracy Physics' |url=https://www.wsj.com/science/physics/the-rise-of-conspiracy-physics-dd79fe36 |access-date=11 September 2026 |work=The Wall Street Journal |type=Essay}}</ref>
